cards.title: A Translational Porcine Model Linking Brain 5-HT2A Receptor Occupancy to Psychedelic-like Behaviour
cards.post: Aim: Establish a translational pig model that links drug dose and plasma concentration to brain 5-HT2A receptor occupancy, so that behavioural doses can be chosen pharmacologically. Methods: Pigs were dosed with five 5-HT2A agonists and two antagonists; brain 5-HT2A occupancy was measured with [11C]Cimbi-36 PET and in vitro, and headshake behaviour was recorded at occupancy levels tied to psychedelic experience in humans. Results: Occupancy correspondence with human data was good across compounds. At human-relevant occupancy, all five agonists induced headshakes, including lisuride and 2-Br-LSD, which are otherwise considered non-psychedelic. Conclusion: Human-relevant 5-HT2A occupancy produces psychedelic-like behaviour in pigs, validating the model for translational dosing of novel 5-HT2A compounds.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your [11C]Cimbi-36 PET work and the question of which occupancy levels are psychedelic in humans.

cards.title: Ayahuasca and Major Depressive Disorder: Examining the Role of the Default Mode Network in Its Therapeutic Potential
cards.post: Aim: Examine the role of the default mode network in the therapeutic potential of ayahuasca for major depressive disorder. Methods: Narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar literature on DMN connectivity in depression and on the neurological and clinical effects of ayahuasca and DMT, prioritising primary research. Results: DMN connectivity findings in depression are inconsistent, with both increases and decreases reported. Ayahuasca studies show changed connectivity and small trials report rapid symptom reduction, but sample sizes are small and mechanisms unclear. Conclusion: Ayahuasca shows antidepressant potential, but controlled research is needed on its long-term effects, safety, and relation to DMN function; MAO-A inhibition may be an alternative mechanism.
cards.why_you: Links ayahuasca, DMN connectivity and depression, close to your interest in psychedelics as treatments for mood disorders.

cards.title: Unmixing the psychedelic connectome: Brain network traits of psilocybin.
cards.post: Aim: Test whether the psilocybin-induced connectome is a composite of dissociable connectivity patterns rather than one global change. Methods: Connectome independent component analysis with multilevel resampling applied to resting-state fMRI from healthy volunteers given psilocybin, relating traits to plasma psilocin and a divergent thinking task. Results: Two empirically uncorrelated functional connectivity traits emerged: one scaled with plasma psilocin concentration, and a second was associated with poorer performance on a visual divergent thinking task. Conclusion: The acute psilocybin state appears to involve co-occurring, dissociable connectivity patterns, supporting decompositional connectomic approaches.
cards.why_you: Brings a data-driven decomposition of psychedelic connectivity that fits your neurodynamics and whole-brain modelling interests.

cards.title: Psilocybin Reconfigures Cortical Dynamics Across Temporal, Spatial, and Hierarchical Scales
cards.post: Aim: Clarify the spatial and temporal origins of increased signal irregularity in psychedelic fMRI studies. Methods: Brain entropy was quantified with sample entropy in 57 paired PsiConnect participants and tested against BOLD surrogates (zero-lag covariance and phase randomisation), with replication in a seven-person crossover cohort. Results: Spatial and temporal entropy rose after psilocybin with reduced local synchrony and shorter intrinsic timescales. Surrogates reproduced the spatial and temporal entropy changes, and the measured increases recurred in the replication cohort. Conclusion: Linking entropy to spatial coordination and temporal persistence explains how psilocybin reorganises cortical dynamics across scales.
cards.why_you: Speaks directly to your EEG complexity and criticality work, applied to psilocybin fMRI.

cards.title: A Pharmacological Basis for Some Bad LSD "Trips"?
cards.post: Aim: Tests whether a metabolite of LSD explains the delayed paranoid phase of LSD intoxication. Methods: Synthesis of 13- and 14-hydroxy-LSD and in vitro receptor testing at the human dopamine D4 receptor. Results: 13-hydroxy-LSD was about 380 times more potent than LSD at the D4 receptor (EC50 36 pM versus 14 nM). Conclusion: 13-hydroxy-LSD may contribute to the delayed dopaminergic phase of LSD action, but in vivo formation and central effects remain unknown.
cards.why_you: Offers a receptor-level hypothesis for the delayed phase of LSD action that bears on your interest in dopaminergic and serotonergic psychedelic pharmacology.

cards.title: DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility correlate with mystical experiences and positive emotionality
cards.post: Aim: To test whether DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility relate to mystical and emotional psychedelic experiences. Methods: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study in 25 healthy participants receiving inhaled DMT (60 mg) or active placebo (0.6 mg), with aberrant salience, suggestibility and psychedelic experience questionnaires. Results: Compared with placebo, DMT increased all aberrant salience factors, most suggestibility modalities and most psychedelic factors. Aberrant salience correlated widely with psychedelic experiences, particularly mystical and positive emotional factors. Conclusion: DMT induces both psychosis- and therapy-relevant processes, with the link to mystical experience possibly indirect and emotionality playing a more central role.
cards.why_you: Adds DMT evidence to the psychedelic clinical pharmacology strand, linking suggestibility and emotion to the mystical experiences your DMT work touches.

cards.title: A signaling signature distinguishes hallucinogenic from non-hallucinogenic psychedelics.
cards.post: Aim: Determine whether hallucinogenic serotonergic psychedelics differ from non-hallucinogenic analogues at the level of intracellular phosphorylation signalling. Methods: Phosphoproteomic profiling of neural cells treated with chemically diverse serotonergic psychedelics and close non-hallucinogenic analogues, with follow-up of FOXK2 phosphorylation and lactate measurements. Results: Psychedelics produced coordinated phosphorylation changes across many proteins, with a signature separating hallucinogenic from non-hallucinogenic compounds. Hallucinogenic compounds, but not analogues, increased lactate accumulation. Conclusion: Under defined in vitro conditions, hallucinogenic and non-hallucinogenic compounds engage separable signalling architectures; the dataset is offered as a resource.
cards.why_you: Bears on the hallucinogenic versus non-hallucinogenic distinction you study in psychedelic pharmacology and tryptamine chemistry.

cards.title: Autistic adults’ attitudes toward ketamine, MDMA, LSD, psilocybin and antidepressants: a cross-sectional survey
cards.post: Aim: Describe how Autistic adults perceive harm, efficacy and willingness to try psilocybin, MDMA, ketamine, LSD and antidepressants. Methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey of 128 Autistic adults (October 2021 to July 2022), rating each substance, with paired comparisons and exploratory associations with self-medication. Results: Psilocybin had the highest proportions endorsing no harm, high efficacy and willingness to try, and differed from the other substances on several measures. Willingness was 17.2 to 21.1 points higher under doctor than peer recommendation. Conclusion: Autistic adults reported more favourable attitudes to psilocybin than antidepressants; these are perceptions, not evidence of comparative efficacy, and recommendation source may matter.
cards.why_you: Relevant to the clinical translation of psychedelic therapies you work towards, in a population rarely studied in this area.

cards.title: Role of Pineal Gland and Melatonin Dysregulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder with a Critical Appraisal of the Endogenous N, N-dimethyltryptamine Hypothesis: A Systematic Review
cards.venue: Journal of Anatomical Society of India
cards.post: Aim: Review pineal and melatonin dysregulation in autism spectrum disorder and critically appraise the endogenous DMT hypothesis. Methods: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, Embase and Web of Science records (2000 to May 2025), with 22 primary studies included and evidence graded with GRADE. Results: Melatonin dysregulation is supported by observational, genetic and clinical evidence, while pineal morphology rests on one neuroimaging study. No included study examined endogenous DMT directly in ASD; the two relevant reports were preclinical. Conclusion: Melatonin-pathway dysfunction is an evidence-supported contributor to ASD-related sleep disturbance, whereas the DMT hypothesis remains theoretical and needs direct human study.
cards.why_you: Touches endogenous DMT and the pineal gland, a question adjacent to your tryptamine and psychedelic research.

cards.title: Novel quantification method for psilocin in brain tissues using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
cards.venue: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
cards.post: Aim: Develops and validates an LC-MS/MS method to quantify psilocin and 4-HIAA in brain tissue. Methods: Chromatography-centred LC-MS/MS approach with matrix dilution, shallower gradient and diverter-valve timing, applied to mouse brain sections from psilocybin and psilocin co-crystal dosing. Results: The method reached a 0.05 ng/mL LLOQ and met validation criteria; no sex or region differences in brain psilocin were found, and psilocybin gave higher psilocin at 10 min than the co-crystal. 4-HIAA was not detected. Conclusion: The validated method enables reliable psilocin quantification in brain tissue, supporting pharmacokinetic work, though the co-crystal difference was not significant.
cards.why_you: A validated brain-tissue psilocin assay would directly support pharmacokinetic characterisation relevant to your psilocybin and tryptamine work.

cards.title: Efficacy, location and kinetics at the 5-HT₂A receptor: A narrative review and testable framework for psychoplastogen design.
cards.post: Aim: Propose a hypothesis-generating framework for designing psychoplastogens that separate neuroplasticity from hallucinogenic effects at the 5-HT2A receptor. Methods: Narrative review of 5-HT2A efficacy, location and kinetics, TrkB binding claims and medicinal chemistry examples, culminating in a proposed set of components with candidate readouts and falsification criteria. Results: Evidence for TrkB-mediated plasticity is disputed and largely preclinical, and no quantitative structure-activity relationship is asserted. The authors propose the term spatiotemporal signalling phenotype with testable components. Conclusion: The framework is a hypothesis-generating medicinal chemistry proposal, not a validated mechanism or a causal model of antidepressant action.
cards.why_you: Directly addresses psychoplastogen design and 5-HT2A signalling, matching your interests in neuroplastogens and tryptamine chemistry.

cards.title: A novel 5-HT2A receptor-linked signalling pathway involving NAADP-mediated lysosomal Ca2+ release
cards.post: Aim: Establish whether the 5-HT2A receptor also signals through NAADP-mediated lysosomal calcium release. Methods: Measurement of cellular NAADP levels, pharmacological NAADP inhibition, direct lysosomal Ca2+ biosensor imaging with psychedelic agonists, and genetic ablation of the pathway in mouse models. Results: Serotonin and a range of psychedelics triggered lysosomal Ca2+ release in a receptor-specific manner. NAADP pathway ablation reduced markers of hallucinogenic and neuroplastic effects in mice. Conclusion: A novel, therapeutically relevant signalling pathway is involved in psychedelic drug action, beyond the canonical G-protein and beta-arrestin routes.

cards.title: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide Induces Transcriptional Changes Opposing Signatures of Brain Ageing and Neurodegeneration.
cards.post: Aim: Asks whether LSD-induced transcriptional changes oppose gene expression signatures of brain ageing and dementia. Methods: Cross-species transcriptomic analysis of chronic LSD in rats and acute LSD in mice, compared with human prefrontal cortex ageing and dementia datasets, plus amyloid-beta experiments in primary cortical cultures. Results: LSD-induced profiles were strongly anti-correlated with human ageing signatures and, less strongly, with dementia signatures, and short-term LSD attenuated amyloid-beta-induced alterations. Conclusion: Provides a transcriptional rationale for investigating LSD and related compounds in brain ageing and neurodegeneration, pointing to mechanisms for future study.

cards.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
cards.venue: The International journal of eating disorders
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is uniform or organised along the cortex's principal functional gradient, and whether it dissociates from cortical thinning. Methods: 44 acutely underweight women with anorexia nervosa and 45 healthy women underwent 3T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labelling with partial-volume correction, analysed across the Schaefer 100-region atlas and compared with cortical thickness and 18 PET/SPECT receptor maps. Results: Perfusion was lower in 97 of 100 regions, maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), and hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A and μ-opioid systems are dense. Conclusion: Cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is graded along the sensorimotor-association axis, dissociable from thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry. The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
cards.why_you: Combines cerebral blood flow, the principal functional gradient and receptor maps, closely matching your neurodynamics and PET neurochemistry interests.

cards.title: Ketamine and psychedelics: A path to Alzheimer's disease prevention?
cards.post: Aim: Whether ketamine and psychedelics can modulate mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology by regulating astrocyte mitochondria. Methods: Narrative review of literature on astrocyte metabolism, stress vulnerability and interactions with neurons, drawn from PubMed, Scopus and Google searches. Results: The reviewed literature suggests astrocyte-linked blood-brain barrier disruption, impaired glymphatic clearance, reduced glutamate uptake and synaptic loss can exacerbate amyloid-β accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation. Ketamine and psychedelics may act on astrocyte mitochondria via NMDA, TrkB, sigma-1 and 5-HT2A receptors, potentially supporting neuronal metabolism. Conclusion: Astrocyte mitochondrial regulation offers a testable framework, but disease-modifying potential requires experimental validation and controlled clinical trials.

cards.title: Roots to Thrive risk and readiness assessment: a practice-based intake and decision-support framework for psychedelic-assisted therapy.
cards.post: Aim: To develop and describe a trauma-informed readiness and risk assessment framework for community-based psychedelic-assisted therapy intake. Methods: Multi-year practice-based quality improvement process from 2020 within a community psychedelic-assisted therapy programme and a university graduate setting, using iterative clinical application, consultation and feedback. Results: The framework integrates biomedical, psychological, relational, cultural, ecological and transpersonal domains to support contextual intake decisions, with reported gains in shared language and alignment with community practice. Conclusion: The framework shifts screening from exclusion towards readiness and risk matched to supports, though it is not yet psychometrically validated and was developed in one setting.

cards.title: The spatial distribution of glioblastoma correlates with specific neurotransmitter maps
cards.post: Aim: To test whether the spatial distribution of glioblastoma follows the normative neurotransmitter and receptor architecture of the healthy brain. Methods: Retrospective study of 96 glioblastoma patients (mean age 62.2 years) from Padova University Hospital, with parcel-wise lesion frequency maps compared to normative PET neurotransmitter maps across two atlases using Neuromaps and spatially constrained null models. cards.title: 5-HT2A receptor deletion is associated with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin levels and anxiety-like behavior in BALB/c mice
cards.post: Aim: Investigates whether constitutive loss of 5-HT2A receptors alters anxiety-like behaviour and hippocampal parvalbumin interneuron proteins in BALB/c mice. cards.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Cancer-Related Psychological and Existential Distress in Adults with Cancer: An Integrative Systematic Review.
cards.venue: Journal of pain & palliative care pharmacotherapy
cards.post: Aim: Evaluates evidence on the safety, efficacy and therapeutic impact of psilocybin-assisted therapy for cancer-related psychological and existential distress. Methods: Integrative systematic review following PRISMA guidelines of 11 reports from six clinical cohorts, searched August to October 2025, with MMAT appraisal. Results: Single moderate-to-high psilocybin doses produced rapid, enduring reductions in depression, anxiety and existential distress lasting 2 to 6 months, and up to 4.5 years in some cases; no serious adverse events were reported. cards.title: Effects of 5-HT2A Receptor Activation on Oxycodone Demand after Short and Long Access Self-Administration in Male and Female Rats.
cards.post: Aim: Whether 5-HT2A receptor activation by DOI reduces oxycodone demand after short or long access self-administration in male and female rats. Methods: Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats with jugular catheters self-administered oxycodone (0.1 mg/kg/infusion) under short or long access; DOI, volinanserin and SB242084 were tested using a threshold demand procedure with exponentiated demand analysis. Results: DOI dose-dependently reduced oxycodone demand in short-access rats in both sexes. After long access, low DOI doses reduced demand while the highest doses enhanced reinforcement; most effects were blocked by volinanserin, which itself reduced demand in long-access rats. Conclusion: Hallucinogenic 5-HT2A activation reduces oxycodone demand in a sex- and access-dependent way, and nonselective phenethylamines may prove less useful than selective agents.

cards.title: Integrating Transformative and Existential Strategies into Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy: A Multi-Study Analysis of EMDR, 3MDR, and Psychedelic-Assisted Group Therapy
cards.venue: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
cards.post: Aim: To test whether transformation strategies within trauma therapies help patients reach deeper existential aspects of suffering, and how interpersonal interaction and transformation contribute to accessing deeper pain and meaning. Methods: Thesis combining a secondary qualitative analysis of 18 psychiatric outpatients with suicidal ideation treated with 12 sessions of web-based EMDR, and a mixed-methods single case study of 3MDR for PTSD in a person with dissociative identity disorder, with follow-up interviews. Results: Three existential themes emerged in the EMDR cohort: self-against-self, the anguish of being, and existential despair. In the 3MDR case, PTSD, anxiety and depression scores improved, with reported resolution of existential themes and post-traumatic growth. Conclusion: The authors suggest many people with chronic suicidality face existential crises rarely addressed in manualised therapies, and that adapted, transformative approaches may be needed. Findings come from a small sample and a single case.

cards.title: Multimodal PET/MR imaging in Alzheimer's disease: A comparative study of structural, metabolic, synaptic and perfusion measures.
cards.venue: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
cards.post: Aim: To compare structural, metabolic, synaptic and perfusion PET/MR measures for detecting neurodegeneration and discriminating Alzheimer's disease from healthy volunteers. Methods: 36 biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's patients underwent 18F-FDG, 18F-SynVesT-1 (SV2A) PET/MR and neuropsychological testing, with cortical thickness, ASL perfusion and volumetry compared against a healthy cohort using cross-validated classification. Results: 18F-FDG PET showed large reductions and the best discrimination (AUC 0.94). Cortical thickness, SV2A PET and volumetry gave similar performance (AUC 0.81-0.86), while ASL was weakest (AUC 0.72) and absent in MCI. Conclusion: Multimodal measures show overlapping but distinct patterns, with synaptic and structural abnormalities present in MCI and perfusion deficits emerging only in dementia-stage disease.

cards.title: Sample size critically shapes the reliability of EEG case-control findings in psychiatry.
cards.post: Aim: Quantify how sample size affects the reliability of EEG case-control findings across psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 2,874 participants aged 5–18 years, including ADHD, autism, anxiety, learning disorders and controls, with spectral, temporal and complexity features compared across repeated random subsamples of varying size. Results: Small samples gave unstable, inflated and highly variable effect sizes, while larger samples converged on consistent but small effects. Statistical power rose steeply with sample size, while false positive rates stayed relatively stable. Conclusion: Sample size critically shapes EEG case-control outcomes, and conventional case-control designs may be limited for biomarker discovery in psychiatry.

cards.title: A staged microstructural mechanism of electroconvulsive therapy: disruption, potentiation, and rewiring.
cards.post: Aim: Whether electroconvulsive therapy works through a staged process of disruption followed by neuroplastic potentiation and network rewiring, tested with longitudinal multishell diffusion MRI. Methods: Densely sampled longitudinal multishell diffusion MRI in 22 people with depression receiving ECT and 15 matched healthy controls, with scans before and after the first session, 7-14 days after the last session, and at 6 months; 141 scans analysed. Results: ECT increased hindered diffusion and decreased free water, mainly in right-lateralised grey matter, consistent with neuroplastic remodelling rather than oedema. Clinical improvement was linked to increased white matter restricted diffusion, most strongly between the second and third time points. Conclusion: The findings give in vivo human evidence for a staged disruption-rewiring process underlying ECT, a framework for how perturbation may become therapeutic reorganisation.

cards.title: Acute Effects of Prolonged Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation on Cortical Excitability: A Randomized Crossover TMS-EEG Study
cards.post: Aim: Whether a single session of prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation changes cortical oscillations and TMS-evoked potentials in healthy males. Methods: Randomised sham-controlled crossover trial in 40 healthy males receiving active or sham piTBS over left DLPFC, with inter-train EEG analysed in 37 participants and TMS-evoked potentials, working memory and attention measured in all 40. Results: Left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks under active versus sham stimulation (interaction p = .014). No TEP clusters differed between conditions; exploratory analyses showed frontal N100 decrease and posterior N100 increase within active piTBS. Behavioural outcomes did not change. Conclusion: A single active piTBS session modulated frontal theta between trains; whether this relates to cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes remains to be tested.

cards.post: Aim: To describe a standardised mouse preparation enabling intracisternal tracer delivery and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI across awake and anaesthetised states. cards.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
cards.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
cards.post: Aim: To determine how single-pulse TMS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex affects single-neuron activity in deep cortical and subcortical structures in humans. Methods: Intracranial microelectrode recordings of 185 single neurons in four neurosurgical patients during single-pulse TMS to left dlPFC, with artifact cleaning enabling spike resolution from 8 ms, alongside TMS-evoked potentials from depth macroelectrodes. Results: Single-pulse TMS elicited time-locked responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated, 19% suppressed, 1% both), in putamen and thalamus among other regions. Putative inhibitory striato-thalamic neurons were facilitated, while excitatory and limbic neurons were suppressed with slower time courses. Conclusion: The authors propose dlPFC TMS recruits many neurons across bilateral cortical and subcortical regions, selectively boosting inhibitory firing in executive networks while suppressing limbic drive. Data come from four patients.

cards.title: SV2A PET imaging in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonism: A systematic review of neuroimaging methodologies and regional findings.
cards.post: Aim: To review neuroimaging methods and regional findings from SV2A PET in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonian disorders. Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science; 14 studies using validated SV2A PET radiotracers in parkinsonian populations; risk of bias with QUADAS-2; narrative synthesis as heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results: In PD the substantia nigra was most affected, with striatal involvement in advanced disease. In PSP and CBD synaptic loss was widespread and exceeded grey matter atrophy, falling about 3-4% per year in some longitudinal regions. In MSA infratentorial involvement predominated, with AUC up to 0.99. Conclusion: The authors conclude SV2A PET shows disease-specific presynaptic patterns supporting its use as a diagnostic and monitoring biomarker. They call for methodological harmonisation and longitudinal multicentre studies.

cards.title: Immediate transcranial magnetic stimulation-evoked potentials reveal short-latency intracortical inhibition.
cards.post: Aim: Test whether immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials give a more direct measure of short-latency intracortical inhibition than MEP-based SICI. Methods: Sixteen healthy volunteers received the standard SICI paired-pulse protocol over motor cortex while immediate TEPs (1–10 ms) and MEPs were recorded, with SICF interval conditions compared. Results: SICI suppressed later iTEP components but not the earliest, and suppression was similar at SICF peaks and troughs. iTEP suppression correlated with MEP suppression, while N15 suppression behaved differently. Conclusion: The authors conclude that MEP-based SICI does not index global motor cortical inhibition but reflects circuit-specific inhibition that iTEPs can probe more directly.

cards.title: 3p-C-NETA: A Versatile Theranostic Chelator Platform Enabling Al18F- and 177Lu-Labeled SSTR2-Targeted Radioligands.
cards.post: Aim: To evaluate 3p-C-NETA-TATE as a theranostic precursor that supports both Al18F and lutetium-177 labelling for SSTR2-targeted radioligands. cards.title: Efficacy Evaluation of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation at Individual Frequency for Patients With Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness: A Preliminary Study Based on Mismatch Negative Amplitude.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether rTMS at an individually selected frequency, guided by mismatch negativity amplitude, improves consciousness in prolonged disorders of consciousness. Methods: Double-blind randomised controlled study of 29 patients; experimental group received individual frequency selection (5, 10 or 15 Hz) based on optimal MMN response, controls received fixed 10 Hz; 4 weeks of rTMS targeting the left mastoid alongside routine rehabilitation. Results: All groups improved. The 15 Hz group (n = 7) had the largest gains (CRS-R 4.71 to 9.29), with greater net improvement than controls (Z = -1.998, p = 0.046). MMN amplitude increased in the 5 Hz and 10 Hz experimental subgroups versus controls. Conclusion: The authors suggest individualised rTMS frequency guided by MMN may aid consciousness recovery and that MMN may be an objective biomarker. The very small subgroups and preliminary design limit inference.

cards.title: The Multi-Objective Computational Design and Prioritization of Novel TSPO PET Radioligands for Improved Inflammation Imaging after Traumatic Brain Injury
cards.post: Aim: Design and prioritise novel TSPO PET radioligands with improved physicochemistry for imaging neuroinflammation after traumatic brain injury. Methods: Cheminformatic pipeline benchmarking eight second-generation ligands, generating a 1,922-analogue haloalkylated dataset from emapunil, then PBPK modelling, plasma-input Logan analysis, ADMET, molecular dynamics and retrosynthesis. Results: Analogue A7 showed a 5.4-fold higher partition coefficient and fourfold higher brain-plasma ratio than the reference in PBPK simulations, with stable Logan estimates and significantly more pocket contacts in molecular dynamics. It was the only non-dominated candidate in Pareto analysis, although one synthetic terminal remained unresolved. Conclusion: A7 is the strongest candidate, demonstrating the value of a cohesive cheminformatic pipeline for PET radioligand development, though synthesis remains to be confirmed.

cards.title: Working memory neural correlates after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression: a randomized placebo-controlled functional magnetic resonance imaging study.
cards.post: Aim: To examine working memory behaviour and fMRI activation after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression versus healthy volunteers. Methods: Secondary analysis of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 unmedicated treatment-resistant depression participants and 19 healthy volunteers, given ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo with 3T fMRI during an N-back task. Results: Ketamine significantly reduced depression scores versus placebo (p < 0.01), but N-back performance did not differ by drug condition. Region-specific activation changes were observed, including reduced parieto-occipital junction activation after ketamine. Conclusion: Ketamine's antidepressant effect occurred without significant working memory change, though task-related regional changes were seen. Modest sample size and exploratory ROI analyses limit interpretation.

cards.title: The Effects of Methylphenidate on the EEG of Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
cards.post: Aim: To determine the effects of methylphenidate alone on resting EEG spectral power in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, including the gamma band. Methods: Fifty children with AD/HD and 50 typically developing children aged 8-12 had eyes-closed resting EEG before and 1.5 hours after 10 mg methylphenidate; absolute and relative power was computed across delta to gamma bands. Results: Unmedicated, the AD/HD group showed elevated delta and posterior theta, reduced relative alpha, and reduced global gamma compared with controls. Methylphenidate increased global beta and relative gamma power. Conclusion: Methylphenidate increased fast-wave activity, but it is unclear whether this counts as normalisation of the EEG.

cards.title: Cannabinoid receptor type 1 availability in individuals with a history of childhood trauma: a positron emission tomography study.
cards.post: Aim: Compare CB1 receptor availability in adults with childhood trauma against healthy controls using PET. Methods: Twenty-two adults with childhood trauma and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent [11C]OMAR PET, with linear models for global, amygdala, hippocampal and frontal regions. cards.title: Rotigotine Behenate ameliorates depression in Parkinson's disease through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether rotigotine behenate ameliorates depression in Parkinson's disease and to identify the anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective mechanisms involved. Methods: A combined MPTP and chronic unpredictable mild stress model in male C57BL/6 mice, compared with fluoxetine, with behavioural assays, neurotransmitter measures in striatum and prefrontal cortex, and NF-κB, BDNF/TrkB and dendritic spine analyses; QNZ was used to inhibit NF-κB. Results: Rotigotine behenate improved motor and depressive-like behaviour and restored regional dopamine and serotonin balance. It suppressed NF-κB/NLRP3 neuroinflammation and activated BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β signalling, reversing spine loss. NF-κB inhibition only partly reproduced these effects. Conclusion: Rotigotine behenate alleviates depression in Parkinson's disease preclinically through anti-inflammatory and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection, with some NF-κB-independent mechanisms.

cards.title: Negative allosteric modulation of α5-GABAA receptors engages dynamic cortical glutamatergic and GABAergic mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior in mice.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether negative allosteric modulation of α5-GABAA receptors with basmisanil produces ketamine-like antidepressant actions via specific medial prefrontal cortex cell populations. Methods: Mice exposed to chronic stress; behavioural testing of motivation, hedonia and coping; c-Fos ensemble mapping; signalling and synaptic protein analyses; chemogenetic silencing of CaMKII pyramidal neurons and GABAergic interneurons at different time points. Results: Basmisanil rapidly and durably facilitated behaviour and reversed chronic stress deficits. It preferentially recruited D1R- and SST-expressing cells, increased Erk and Akt-mTOR signalling and synaptic proteins, and early pyramidal silencing blocked both rapid and sustained effects while interneuron silencing blocked sustained effects. Conclusion: Early pyramidal activation initiates rapid plasticity, whereas GABAergic interneurons sustain and express the lasting antidepressant-like effects, highlighting interneuron circuits as targets.

cards.title: Ketamine-Augmented Hypnotherapy.
cards.post: Aim: To describe ketamine-augmented hypnotherapy (KAHT) and report preliminary feasibility and outcome data from an uncontrolled case series. Methods: Narrative review of psychedelic, ketamine-induced and hypnotic states, followed by a description of KAHT: a single 0.5 mg/kg racemic ketamine infusion under hypnotherapeutic guidance, with preliminary data from 89 patients including MEQ and pre-post PHQ-9 in 20. Results: Most patients described calming or psychedelic effects, with highest MEQ scores for transcendence of time and space. PHQ-9 fell significantly (p = 0.048), though not significantly in the clinically depressed subgroup (p = 0.09). Of 20 patients, 12 reported lasting benefit. Conclusion: KAHT appears feasible across diagnoses but responses vary; the uncontrolled design cannot isolate the hypnotherapy contribution, so randomised trials are needed.

cards.title: Transcriptional profiling of antidepressant ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy treatment.
cards.post: Aim: To characterise longitudinal peripheral blood transcriptional changes during ECT and serial ketamine treatment in treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Peripheral blood RNA-seq in 37 ECT patients, 60 ketamine patients and 35 controls at multiple time points; differential expression and WGCNA co-expression network analysis with multiple-comparison correction. Results: No longitudinal changes were detected for individual genes or networks after FDR correction. Baseline comparisons showed immune-related enrichment and one gene (IGKV1-9) differing between ketamine remitters and non-remitters, and several modules differing between ECT patients and controls. Conclusion: Despite clinical improvement, peripheral transcriptional change was limited; pre-treatment differences hint at predictive value, and larger samples are needed.

cards.title: Intravenous ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice: a review of non-randomized evidence on effectiveness and safety.
cards.post: Aim: To review non-randomised evidence on the effectiveness and safety of intravenous racemic ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice. Methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 30 September 2026; 56 non-randomised studies included. Results: Response ranged from 26% to 71% and remission from 14% to 53%, overlapping RCT estimates. Benefits often waned within weeks, attrition was high, blood pressure rises were transient, and serious adverse events and urinary and hepatic outcomes were poorly reported. Conclusion: Durability of benefit and cumulative safety of repeated IV ketamine remain uncertain; systematic safety monitoring and head-to-head and maintenance trials are needed.

cards.title: Proteomic profiling of postmortem prefrontal cortex identifies molecular signatures of borderline personality disorder
cards.post: Aim: To characterise proteomic signatures of borderline personality disorder in postmortem prefrontal cortex. Methods: Label-free proteomics of postmortem prefrontal cortex in 79 individuals (36 with BPD, 43 controls); differential expression, co-expression network, druggability and drug-repositioning analyses; integration with PTSD and MDD datasets. Results: Dysregulation of mitochondrial, immunological and neuroplasticity pathways was observed. A BPD-associated module enriched for secretory and synaptic processes was druggable by SSRIs, and STX7 and RTN4 were conserved differentially expressed proteins across BPD, PTSD and MDD. Conclusion: The study provides initial proteomic insights into BPD in the brain, suggests VEGF signalling as a possible target, and shows convergent signatures with common comorbidities.

cards.title: Gender- and season-specific neural signature revealed by resting EEG in major depressive disorder
cards.post: Aim: Determine how gender and season jointly modulate resting EEG activity in major depressive disorder and whether EEG features predict symptom severity. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 132 people with MDD (67 women, 65 men, aged 18.66-78.00 years) across seasons; power spectral density, fuzzy entropy and transfer entropy; two-way ANOVA and Categorical Boosting regression with SHAP analysis. Results: Neural activity was modulated by gender and season, with peak divergence in winter or summer for women and spring for men. EEG features predicted Beck Depression Inventory scores with high accuracy (r = 0.9405 for women in winter). Conclusion: EEG features may serve as candidate biomarkers, and diagnosis may need to account for seasonal and gender-specific biological rhythms.

cards.title: Abnormalities and plasticity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder: a BOLD fMRI study.
cards.post: Aim: To investigate architecture and activity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder and their change after prolonged abstinence. Methods: BOLD fMRI white matter signals analysed with k-means clustering in individuals with OUD at baseline and follow-up after prolonged abstinence, compared with healthy controls. Results: At baseline the deep frontoparietal network fragmented into the superior longitudinal fasciculus and anterior corona radiata networks, partially recovering after abstinence. Hyperactivation in the deep frontal network and hypoactivation in the frontotemporal-parietal network were present, with the latter negatively correlated with years of opioid use. Conclusion: OUD disrupts white matter network architecture and activity, while prolonged abstinence promotes partial restoration, indicating neuroplastic potential of white matter networks.

cards.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether brain aging, measured as a brain age gap, is elevated in medication-free people with major depressive disorder and whether it depends on age and neuroanatomical phenotype. Methods: Harmonised T1-weighted MRI from 645 medication-free people with a current depressive episode and 645 matched healthy controls across 11 sites; gradient boosting brain age estimation with nested cross-validation and SHAP regional contributions. Results: Major depressive disorder was associated with a higher age-corrected brain age gap than controls (mean difference +2.0 years, Cohen's d -0.289). Gaps were absent before the mid-30s and reached +6.8 years in those aged 55 and older before site adjustment (4.3 years after). Conclusion: Structural brain aging in depression is age-dependent and strongest in a clinically vulnerable phenotype, consistent with but not establishing neuroprogression models.

cards.title: Magnetoencephalography reveals altered synaptic gain linked to functional impairment in adolescents at familial risk for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
cards.post: Aim: To test whether auditory oddball responses and effective connectivity differ in adolescents at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Methods: MEG during a roving oddball paradigm in 15-year-olds: 59 at familial high risk for schizophrenia, 38 for bipolar disorder, and 75 population controls; sensor and source analyses; dynamic causal modelling of effective connectivity. cards.title: An examination of cerebellar perineuronal nets in major depression and child abuse
cards.post: Aim: Test whether a history of child abuse alters perineuronal nets in the human dentate nucleus and in mouse deep cerebellar nuclei. Methods: Post-mortem human dentate nucleus from depressed suicides with or without child abuse history and matched controls, using FISH and immunofluorescence; mice reared under limited-bedding early-life adversity versus standard rearing. Results: Perineuronal net density was unchanged by child abuse in humans and by early-life adversity in mice, and the phenotype of enveloped cells did not differ in the human dentate nucleus. Conclusion: Cerebellar perineuronal nets, which mature early postnatally, do not appear to be affected by child abuse, in contrast to prefrontal findings.

cards.title: Low-Threshold Intermittent Hypoxia Exacerbates LPS-Induced Depressive-Like Behaviors and Cognitive Deficits While Potentiating the Hippocampal STING-TBK1 Pathway.
cards.post: Aim: Determine whether low-threshold intermittent hypoxia worsens LPS-induced depressive-like behaviour, cognitive deficits and hippocampal neuroinflammation. Methods: Adult male mice exposed to low-threshold intermittent hypoxia during systemic LPS challenge; tail suspension, forced swim and sucrose preference tests; Morris water maze; hippocampal STING-TBK1-IRF3 pathway, synaptic markers and cytokine measures. Results: Hypoxia alone did not impair behaviour, but it amplified LPS-induced depressive-like behaviour and cognitive decline. It also intensified STING-TBK1 activation, reduced PSD-95 and synaptophysin, and raised pro-inflammatory cytokines. Conclusion: Hypoxia synergises with systemic inflammation to worsen mood, cognition and neuroinflammation, possibly through hyperactive STING-dependent immune signalling.

cards.title: Lilium–egg yolk composite granules ameliorates depressive-like behaviors in CUMS rats with associated changes in neuroinflammation, gut microbiota, and SCFAs
cards.post: Aim: Assess whether lilium-egg yolk composite granules (BHT) ameliorate depressive-like behaviour in chronically stressed rats through gut microbiota and fatty acid changes. Methods: 72 male SD rats randomised to control, CUMS, three BHT doses or fluoxetine for 28 days; behavioural tests, histology, electron microscopy, cytokine assays, faecal metagenomics and GC-MS of short-chain fatty acids. cards.title: Targeting IL-1 Signaling to Improve Antidepressant Efficacy in a Rodent Model of Postpartum Depression
cards.post: Aim: Test whether IL-1 receptor antagonism improves fluoxetine's effects on neuroplasticity and behaviour in a rodent model of postpartum depression. Methods: Rats given high corticosterone for 21 days postpartum, treated with fluoxetine, anakinra or both; maternal care, forced swim, hippocampal neurogenesis and perineuronal net counts in hippocampus and frontal cortex. Results: Combined treatment reversed corticosterone-induced changes in neurogenesis and perineuronal net numbers, while either drug alone did not. Behavioural passive coping in the forced swim test was not reversed. Conclusion: IL-1 signalling may limit antidepressant-induced neuroplasticity postpartum, and IL-1 receptor antagonism is a promising adjunct, though neuroplastic and behavioural effects dissociated.

cards.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
cards.post: Aim: To develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion framework for identifying EEG features that show discrimination, reliability and cross-cohort consistency in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Methods: Eighteen EEG features assessed across three cohorts: a home-recorded ALS cohort with 170 controls, a clinic-recorded ALS cohort of eight patients, and a healthy test-retest reference of 60 participants, with permutation and bootstrap robustness testing. Results: Gamma power, theta power and spectral entropy met all three criteria. Cross-cohort differences in reliability, such as relative beta power (ICC 0.09 at home versus 0.93 in clinic), were large relative to the disease signal, and the selected set was sensitive to sample composition. Conclusion: Recording setting and protocol differences can outweigh disease-associated EEG signal, so cross-cohort validation is essential before biomarker translation.

cards.title: Introducing the “ASCENT” EEGLAB Plugin: Aperiodic Signal Complexity Estimation for Neurophysiological Time Series
cards.post: Aim: Introduce ASCENT, an open-source EEGLAB plugin for computing entropy, fractal and aperiodic measures on neurophysiological time series. cards.title: Synergistic contributions of periodic and aperiodic cortical activity to motor recovery prediction after stroke.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether periodic and aperiodic resting EEG components predict motor recovery after chronic stroke. Methods: Resting-state EEG (1 minute) recorded at admission and discharge with a portable system in 41 chronic stroke patients, parameterised with spectral decomposition and used in stepwise regression and classification. Results: Ipsilesional alpha-peak activity increased after rehabilitation and correlated with motor gain (r = 0.39). A model of higher individual alpha frequency, steeper aperiodic slope and their interaction predicted recovery (R2 = 0.53; balanced accuracy 88%) and outperformed a delta-alpha ratio. Conclusion: The interaction between periodic and aperiodic activity is a mechanistically meaningful and clinically relevant marker of residual plasticity in chronic stroke.

cards.title: Excitation/Inhibition Balance in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: A Functional MRI Study
cards.post: Aim: Investigate excitation/inhibition-related brain dynamics, indexed by the resting-state Hurst exponent, in people at clinical high risk for psychosis. Methods: Resting-state fMRI from two longitudinal cohorts (PSYSCAN: 190 CHR-P, 115 controls; AMP SCZ: 826 CHR-P, 241 controls); Hurst exponent mapping; comparison with normative receptor distributions; transition analysis in PSYSCAN (21 transitioners). Results: CHR-P individuals had lower whole-brain Hurst exponent than controls, most prominently in somatomotor network and thalamus. Receptor distributions for noradrenaline, serotonin and opioid systems predicted the spatial pattern, and baseline regional values gave above-chance individual prediction of transition. Conclusion: Psychosis vulnerability is linked to reduced Hurst exponent, consistent with less persistent brain dynamics and increased excitability, though transition evidence is preliminary.

cards.title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action.
cards.post: Aim: To explain how atomoxetine reshapes whole-brain dynamics by linking multi-receptor adrenergic and dopaminergic organisation to resting-state functional connectivity. Methods: Pharmacological resting-state fMRI under atomoxetine and placebo combined with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical adrenergic and dopaminergic receptor expression, using receptor similarity and forward simulation. Results: Atomoxetine stabilised connectivity dynamics within a posterior catecholaminergic network. Model parameters converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities, and the drug state was reconstructed from placebo by negative reweighting along that affinity axis. Conclusion: Receptor binding affinity may be a key organising principle linking molecular receptor organisation to brain dynamics under catecholaminergic perturbation.

cards.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
cards.post: Aim: To introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling for estimating effective connectivity across the cortex, brainstem and heart. Methods: Extension of generative causal modelling with a closed-loop brainstem cardiac neural mass model including five brainstem nuclei, a thalamic relay and the sinoatrial node, jointly inverted with simultaneous EEG and ECG during an auditory Go/No-Go task. Results: The framework distinguished granular from agranular microcircuit hypotheses within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy and recovered time-varying synaptic efficacy with latent neuronal dynamics across anticipation, target and inhibition windows. Conclusion: Linking neural and cardiac signals in one generative architecture moves brain-heart research beyond correlation and offers a way to test embodied inference theories.

cards.title: The biological basis underlying the local brain functional changes of taVNS in treating major depressive disorder: An imaging transcriptomics study.
cards.post: Aim: Whether the functional brain changes produced by eight weeks of taVNS in major depression map onto specific gene expression and neurotransmitter receptor patterns. Methods: Prospective single-arm longitudinal cohort of 122 patients with MDD, resting-state fMRI before and after 8 weeks of taVNS; ALFF and ReHo change correlated with HAMD-17 change, linked to Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression via LASSO and to 32 PET receptor maps. Conclusion: taVNS-associated functional changes show spatial enrichment for distinct synaptic and neuroimmune pathways, offering candidate molecular correlates, though the single-arm design limits efficacy inference.

cards.title: Physiological Mechanisms of Yoga on Sleep Architecture and Autonomic Regulation: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
cards.venue: Aathiyoga Indian Journal of Ancient Medicine and Yoga
cards.post: Aim: Systematically review randomised trials of yoga's physiological effects on sleep architecture and autonomic regulation, using objective endpoints. Methods: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of PubMed records from the past five years; four RCTs met criteria; extracted heart rate variability, cardiorespiratory, neuroendocrine, EEG and sleep onset latency data; Cochrane RoB 2 risk-of-bias assessment. cards.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of interoceptive conceptual processing in the human brain.
cards.venue: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
cards.post: Aim: How the strength of interoceptive meaning in verbs shapes the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of conceptual processing. Methods: MEG study with 16 participants in a lexical decision task using high- and low-interoceptive verbs; time-frequency analysis, representational similarity analysis, descriptive source reconstruction and cardiac variability measures. cards.title: Altered directional brain-heart interactions across resting states and frequency bands in schizophrenia.
cards.post: Aim: Whether directional brain-heart interactions differ between patients with schizophrenia and healthy men across resting states and EEG frequency bands. Methods: Simultaneous resting-state EEG and ECG in 33 medicated men with schizophrenia and 29 healthy men, eyes open and eyes closed; directional brain-heart interaction across two coupling directions, two cardiac components and five EEG bands, with permutation and sensitivity analyses. cards.title: Meditation-induced coherence and perennial aging.
cards.post: Aim: Examine how meditation alters scaling behaviour and complexity synchronisation between brain and heart dynamics, using a non-Markovian quantum-like framework. Methods: Theoretical and analytical study applying a non-ergodic self-organisation model to EEG and ECG during Naam Jap meditation; scaling exponent estimation, brain-heart complexity synchronisation and group-level statistics. Conclusion: Meditation induces a coherent state followed by increased physiological complexity, supporting a non-ergodic account of cognition, though the framework is novel and specific.

cards.title: Dissociating Early Heartbeat-Evoked Afferent Gating From Late Associative Failure in Post-Anoxic Coma
cards.post: Aim: Whether the heartbeat-evoked response can separate viable from non-viable cortical function in comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Methods: Multicentre EEG and ECG from 150 comatose post-cardiac arrest patients (discovery n = 100, validation n = 50); sLORETA source localisation and Hilbert-Huang transform with empirical mode decomposition of early (150-300 ms) and late (350-500 ms) post-R-peak windows. Results: Good outcome was linked to a preserved frontocentral deflection near 200 ms localised to the anterior cingulate and anterior insula, with high instantaneous energy and phase alignment. Non-survivors showed a positive shift, energy collapse and phase desynchronisation; late windows showed diffuse dissipation in both groups. Conclusion: Preserved early interoceptive afferent gating to the cingulate and insula, rather than late associative activity, is proposed as an electrophysiological biomarker of viable cortical microcircuitry.

cards.title: Scn2a -deficient mice exhibit serotonergic dysfunction and altered behavioral responses to psilocybin.
cards.venue: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
cards.post: Aim: Tests whether Scn2a deficiency alters behavioural responses to psilocybin and serotonergic system function in mice. cards.title: Changes in wellbeing, self-compassion and alexithymia in a proof of principle trial with MDMA-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder.
cards.post: Aim: To examine whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes alexithymia, self-compassion and well-being in major depressive disorder, and whether effects last. Methods: Open-label proof-of-principle trial with 12 participants with moderate to severe MDD (baseline MADRS 29.6), receiving two MDMA sessions with manualised psychotherapy; outcomes at baseline, 8 weeks and at least 3 months, analysed with linear mixed models. Results: TAS-20 fell by 11.75 post-treatment and 16.42 at follow-up (both p < 0.001). Self-compassion rose (SCS +0.73, p = 0.017; +1.07 at follow-up, p = 0.001). cards.title: Psychedelic Use and Mental Health Diagnosis Shape Attitudes Toward Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy
cards.post: Aim: Whether prior psychedelic use and mental health diagnosis are associated with attitudes towards psychedelic-assisted therapy. Methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online convenience survey of 99 adults aged 21 or older recruited via social media and text messages; t tests and Fisher exact tests comparing groups by prior psychedelic use, diagnosis and healthcare-worker status. cards.post: Aim: Whether ketamine promotes more strategic and efficient approach-avoidance behaviour in healthy adults, compared with lorazepam and no medication. cards.title: Long-term dysregulation of histone acetylation, BDNF expression, and the hippocampal transcriptome in adult rats exhibiting a depressive-like phenotype following repeated chlorpyrifos exposure
cards.post: Aim: To investigate molecular mechanisms underlying a chronic depressive-like phenotype after repeated occupational-like chlorpyrifos exposure in rats. Methods: Adult rats given chlorpyrifos at 5 mg/kg/day for 21 days, assessed three months later; hippocampal Western blotting, ChIP for H3K9ac at the Bdnf promoter IV, and exploratory RNA-sequencing. cards.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
cards.post: Aim: To provide a simulator that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with controllable, disease-specific pattern injection across several neurological disorders, to address scarce and heterogeneous labelled clinical data. Methods: Physiologically motivated baseline generator with band-limited rhythms, ERPs, artifacts and hierarchical variability; region- and severity-specific spectral modulation encoding biomarkers for five disorders; validation via spectral, topographic and multivariate analyses, a convolutional-attention classifier and real clinical EEG from the Temple University Hospital corpus. Results: Simulated signals reproduced expected biomarker directionality, and the classifier reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy. Adding NeuroSim samples to real training data raised accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus controls. Conclusion: NeuroSim is released as open-source software for augmentation, benchmarking and explainable AI in neurological diagnostics, with its clinical utility shown on the cited corpus and two disease comparisons.

cards.title: Deep learning to overcome human error and bias in electrode position extraction in tDCS-fMRI studies
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether a 3D U-Net can automatically extract tDCS electrode positions from PETRA MRI scans, removing human error and bias. Methods: Five U-Net variants benchmarked with five-fold cross-validation on 54 expert-segmented images and across 4,234 images from a multi-site tDCS-fMRI study; automated, semi-automatic and manual extraction of a 3×1 montage compared against expert ground truth. Results: Ungated networks recovered all four electrodes in 97.7% and 96.3% of images, versus 89.0 to 91.2% with attention gates. Automated methods agreed closely (ICC = 0.984, bias 1.3 mm), while manual extraction showed a 6.3 mm systematic offset. Conclusion: The authors release the standard U-Net as open source, arguing automation removes a measurable error source and scales to large datasets.

cards.post: Background: Although diffusion MRI (dMRI) enables detailed mapping of these pathways through tractography, how WM pathways directly facilitate large-scale neural synchronisation remains poorly understood. Conclusion: Together, these findings depict the whole-brain track-level functional organisation of WM tracks and provide a powerful tool to study brain ageing and cognitive decline.

cards.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China.
cards.post: Background: Homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Results: We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. Conclusion: The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility.

cards.post: Background: A carbon price is an effective and cost-efficient policy to mitigate emissions, yet low public acceptance and limited political support remain major barriers to its widespread implementation. Results: By implementing all designs simultaneously with almost 20,000 US residents, this preregistered study shows very small positive but statistically significant effects of behavioural interventions on a set of design-specific proxies of real-world support (Cohen's d = 0.06; 99.5% confidence interval (CI) 0.001 to 0.124) and on 4 out of 5 common measures of stated support … Conclusion: Lastly, we identify strong overconfidence among research teams regarding the expected effects of their interventions and those of their peers, indicating a miscalibration of community expectations.

cards.title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether later-born generations enter old age with better memory and decline more slowly, and whether this explains falling dementia incidence. Methods: Analysis of about 783,000 episodic-memory assessments from about 219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed up to 30 years, including hippocampal volumes. Results: Later-born generations showed higher memory levels in old age and slower subsequent decline, a double advantage large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade fall in dementia incidence. Slower decline was mirrored by lower clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Conclusion: Sustaining the dementia decline requires prevention that protects brain health across the lifespan, starting in childhood.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your interest in brain health across the lifespan and computational psychiatry, though not a direct match to your current work.

cards.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
cards.post: Aim: Whether hippocampal neurons encode word position and context in a way resembling transformer self-attention, in natural speech. Methods: Single-unit recordings from the human hippocampus in n = 10 participants listening to podcasts; analysis of positional encoding and weighted sums of preceding word embeddings, compared with LLM self-attention weights. Results: Hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause using ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Neural responses reflected both a word's lexical semantics and a weighted sum of preceding word embeddings, with weights correlating with LLM self-attention. Conclusion: Contextualisation in the brain may use vectorial shifts resembling attentional reweighting in LLMs, highlighting the mesial temporal lobe in the language network.
cards.why_you: Single-unit human hippocampal recordings and neural–model comparisons are relevant to your interest in neurodynamics and computational approaches to brain function.

cards.title: Anterior cingulate cortex neurons parse speakers in a natural cocktail party.
cards.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
cards.post: Aim: How anterior cingulate cortex neurons parse social partners' vocalisations in a noisy, natural colony environment. Methods: Single-neuron recordings from ACC (area 24) in freely moving marmosets engaged in spontaneous vocal exchanges within a colony setting. Results: ACC neurons selectively encoded calls from a social partner versus other callers, preserved during temporal overlap. Population activity also represented vocal production, call type and turn-taking context. Conclusion: ACC neurons appear to parse conspecific speakers during natural communication, linking auditory scene analysis with social monitoring.
cards.why_you: Freely moving single-unit recordings in a natural social context sit outside your human imaging work but connect to your interest in brain–body and social neuroscience.

cards.title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment.
cards.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
cards.post: Aim: Whether morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment than materially motivated ones. Methods: Ten studies combining federal offender data (over 30,000 offenders), judgment experiments and economic games with general-population and offender participants. Results: Moral motives predicted higher recidivism while material motives predicted lower recidivism. Morally motivated crimes were less sensitive to punishment across crime types and consequence manipulations, and players taking money for moral reasons were less deterred by fines. Conclusion: Punishment may deter morally motivated offending less effectively, with implications for sentencing and restorative justice approaches.
cards.why_you: Largely outside your fields; a neuroscientist might find it interesting as a psychological account of how motives modulate sensitivity to aversive consequences.

cards.title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit.
cards.post: Aim: How nitric oxide signalling gates a UV-avoidance circuit in the annelid larva Platynereis dumerilii. Methods: Genetic mutants, behavioural assays, cell-specific expression of nitric oxide synthase, and mathematical modelling of phototransduction and circuit dynamics. Results: UV stimulation activated nitric oxide production in interneurons, which signalled retrogradely to ciliary photoreceptors and sustained their activation. NOS mutants showed defective retrograde signalling, ciliary activation and UV avoidance. Conclusion: Retrograde nitric oxide signalling gates a synaptic circuit and provides short-term memory of UV exposure to guide avoidance behaviour.
cards.why_you: Retrograde gaseous signalling and circuit gating in a simple photoreceptive system is relevant to your interest in neuromodulation and dynamics.

cards.title: Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior.
cards.post: Aim: Whether Rhodopsin 7, a widely expressed non-canonical photoreceptor, shapes light-responsive behaviour in Drosophila. Methods: Expression mapping, behavioural assays of activity under light and dark, constitutively active RH7 strains, and phylogenetic comparisons across arthropods. Results: RH7 detects temporal luminance changes and guides rapid responses. Flies lacking RH7 were less active in the dark phase, while constitutively active RH7 increased activity. RH7 appears ancient across panarthropods. Conclusion: RH7 acts as a melanopsin-like sensor shaping behaviour and represents an evolutionary intermediate in non-visual light perception.
cards.why_you: Non-visual light sensing shaping daily activity patterns connects loosely to your interest in circadian and non-image-forming brain function.

cards.title: A shared interbacterial membrane underlies mycobacterial cording.
cards.post: Aim: How individual mycobacterial cells coordinate growth, division and adhesion to form serpentine cords. Methods: Live-cell fluorescence microscopy combined with cryo-electron tomography of virulent mycobacteria. Results: Snapping division generates a shared interbacterial membrane between daughter cells, extending laterally during cord formation. Lipid composition and an interleaflet density associated with virulence-factor secretion were observed in M. tuberculosis. Conclusion: A multi-bacterial membrane architecture provides the structural basis for cording and collective behaviours such as mechanical stability and phage resistance.

cards.title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress.
cards.post: Aim: Whether early-life stress and nerve injury interact to produce female-specific circuit sensitisation driving chronic pain vulnerability. Methods: Mouse study of social isolation and nerve injury, measuring synaptic gain and activity in the paraventricular thalamus to central amygdala pathway, with chemogenetic inhibition and activation. Results: Social isolation plus nerve injury amplified synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the pathway in female but not male mice. Pathway inhibition rescued behaviour, while sustained or phasic activation induced hypersensitivity or avoidance. Conclusion: A latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state, unmasked by injury, may transform early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

cards.title: An engineered cohesion system reduces errors in aged mammalian eggs.
cards.post: Aim: Whether an engineered artificial cohesion system can reduce premature sister chromatid separation in aged mammalian eggs. Methods: Creation of an artificial cohesion system in aged mouse eggs, with a separase-cleavable sequence for scheduled deactivation, plus a proof-of-principle test tethering human chromosomes. Results: The artificial cohesion system reduced premature sister chromatid separation in aged mouse eggs and could be adapted to tether human chromosomes. Conclusion: Provides a proof of principle for future approaches to reduce premature separation in eggs from women of advanced reproductive age.

cards.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
cards.post: Aim: How an intronic SVA retrotransposon in TAF1 contributes to X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP). Methods: Genomic rewriting of a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the 78-kb XDP patient-derived allele in mouse embryonic stem cells and mice, with chromatin and transcriptome profiling and CRISPRa activation. Results: The intronic SVA reduced hybrid TAF1 mRNA, downregulated TATA-box genes and triggered apoptosis. Intronic SVAs were actively transcribed and impeded elongation. Neuronal humanisation caused male lethality and striatal atrophy, and CRISPRa activation restored viability. Conclusion: Boosting TAF1 transcription may be a therapeutic approach for XDP, which is associated with striatal degeneration.
cards.why_you: Striatal neurodegeneration and transcriptional mechanisms in a human disease model are loosely relevant to your neuroscience interests.

cards.title: Increased signal diversity/complexity of spontaneous EEG, but not evoked EEG responses, in ketamine-induced psychedelic state in humans
cards.post: Aim: Whether EEG signal diversity, measured spontaneously and evoked by TMS, changes under sub-anaesthetic ketamine and relates to subjective experience. Methods: Open-label within-subject study in 10 healthy volunteers with 62-channel EEG, recording TMS-evoked responses (PCI) and spontaneous EEG (Lempel-Ziv complexity, amplitude and synchrony coalition entropy) before and during sub-anaesthetic ketamine. Results: No significant change in evoked complexity (PCI). All spontaneous signal diversity measures increased under ketamine, correlating with subjective altered states, and were higher with eyes open than closed. Conclusion: Spontaneous and evoked complexity may reflect complementary aspects; ketamine may raise conscious-content complexity while leaving overall capacity for consciousness largely unchanged.
cards.why_you: Directly matches your work on ketamine, EEG complexity and TMS-EEG perturbation measures.

cards.title: Neural Sources and Underlying Mechanisms of Neural Responses to Heartbeats, and their Role in Bodily Self-consciousness: An Intracranial EEG Study
cards.post: Aim: Whether heartbeat-evoked potentials arise from neural sources and mechanisms that can be localised, and whether they relate to bodily self-consciousness. Methods: Two intracranial EEG experiments in patients, examining heartbeat-locked phase distributions and spectral power across recording sites, and HEP modulation during an experimentally induced altered sense of self-identification. Results: Shortly after heartbeat onset, phases were significantly concentrated in about 10% of sites, mainly insula and operculum, without increased spectral power, suggesting phase resetting. Insula HEP modulations reflected altered self-identification. Conclusion: The authors conclude that HEPs arise largely through phase resetting and that their insular modulation supports a functional role in self-consciousness.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your interest in heart-brain coupling and interoception, offering intracranial evidence on where cardiac-evoked responses originate.

cards.post: tvb-root 3.0.0a1 is an early alpha of a multi-model simulation framework with a pure Python backend, Numba code generation and parameter sweeps, plus tutorial notebooks. APIs may still change.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your whole-brain and neural mass modelling interests, though the release is early and unstable.

cards.title: nibabel 5.5.0 released
cards.post: nibabel 5.5.0 is a feature release of the Python neuroimaging I/O library, adding DICOM mixed-orientation filtering, complex image support in get_fdata and reorientation improvements. It requires Python 3.11 or later.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your imaging analysis code if you read and reorient NIfTI or CIFTI files in Python.

cards.title: mriqc 26.1.0 released
cards.post: MRIQC 26.1.0, the first minor release of the 26.x series, adds FLAIR image support and fixes a head mask issue that changed background IQMs for anatomical runs. Available via Docker and PyPI (Python 3.13 or newer).
cards.why_you: A quality-control tool for MRI data, useful if your PET or multimodal pipelines draw on BIDS-formatted anatomical and functional scans.
